title: Sweet Dee Gets Audited

jokes.text: Hey, guys, why are the urinals filled with rocks? / 'Cause I put a bunch of rocks in 'em.
jokes.setup: Someone notices urinals filled with rocks and asks for a reasonable explanation.
jokes.punchline: Frank's explanation is not an explanation at all — he simply restates the obvious with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The absurd logic chain (broken urinals → ice → broken ice machine → rocks) delivered deadpan is a strong cold open. The non-answer answer is well-executed character comedy for Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, 'cause I put a bunch of rocks in 'em.

jokes.text: Frank's escalating explanation: ice machine broke, so now using rocks — 'You know that doesn't make any sense, right? Replacing the ice with rocks?'
jokes.setup: Frank explains his logic: urinals needed ice, ice machine broke, so he used rocks as a substitute.
jokes.punchline: The ice served a sanitary purpose; rocks serve none. The logic is so broken it loops back around to seeming intentional.
jokes.explanation: Frank's pseudo-logic is a great character joke — he genuinely believes this is a reasonable substitution. The straight-man calling it out sharpens the absurdity. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, you know how they were broken, so I was, like, filling them with ice. Now the ice machine's broken, so I'm just filling them up with rocks.

jokes.text: The ice actually served a purpose... Oh, oh, God! Oh, something just dripped in my mouth!
jokes.setup: Dennis is mid-sentence making a rational point about the ice when the ceiling leaks on him.
jokes.punchline: The universe physically interrupts his reasoning with a drip of gross ceiling water into his mouth.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing — cutting off the rational voice with physical grossness. The disgust reaction lands well and sets the tone for the bar's state of decay.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, something just dripped in my mouth!

jokes.text: What'd it taste like?
jokes.setup: Dennis is horrified after ceiling water dripped into his mouth.
jokes.punchline: Frank's only response is morbid curiosity about the taste, entirely missing the point of Dennis's disgust.
jokes.explanation: Four words, completely in character for Frank — no empathy, only base curiosity. The economy is perfect and the character integration is exceptional. Frank's detachment from normal human concern is crystallized in a single question. Genuinely comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its precision.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What'd it taste like?

jokes.text: What's up, bitches? New scooter. My surrogate money came in. 30 G's, babies.
jokes.setup: The gang is mid-argument about bar finances and Frank docking paychecks.
jokes.punchline: Dee bursts in riding a scooter, announcing her surrogate baby scheme paid off — total tonal whiplash.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny entrance — Dee is gleefully self-congratulatory about an objectively terrible life decision. The contrast with the mundane bar argument is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Who gives a shit what it tasted like, Frank?

jokes.text: Oh, sweet. Where's our cut?
jokes.setup: Dee announces she made $30K from a surrogacy scheme.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately and shamelessly demands a cut of money from a pregnancy he had nothing to do with.
jokes.explanation: Quick and efficient — perfectly captures the gang's entitlement. The brevity is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What's up, bitches?

jokes.text: You did nothing for nine months.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie argue they worked their asses off on Dee's surrogacy scheme and deserve a cut.
jokes.punchline: Dee correctly points out they did literally nothing — the irony being she's the one who was pregnant.
jokes.explanation: Clean retort, good economy, but fairly predictable counter-argument. Gets a solid laugh without being exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: My surrogate money came in. 30 G's, babies.

jokes.text: I made all the contacts, I pushed that little monkey out and now I'm going to be claiming him as a dependent and getting tax breaks for the next 18 years. So you talk about a scheme? How's that for a long-term scheme, bitches? You guys all better eat a dick, 'cause Sweet Dee beat the system.
jokes.setup: Dee is defending her surrogacy scheme as a legitimate con.
jokes.punchline: Dee's grand celebration of 'beating the system' by fraudulently claiming a baby she gave away as a dependent — which we immediately see backfires — delivered with maximum self-satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: The irony is immediately set up for destruction — we know she's already failed by the next scene. 'Sweet Dee beat the system' becomes a rewatch joke once you know the IRS is at the door. Good character work and a solid quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What the hell are you talking about? You did nothing for nine months.

jokes.text: Whatever god you're selling, I ain't buying it.
jokes.setup: An official-looking woman approaches Dee's door. Dee assumes she's a religious proselytizer.
jokes.punchline: The woman is from the IRS — Dee's bravado is immediately deflated.
jokes.explanation: Solid misdirection setup — Dee's confident dismissal reads as an ironic character beat given she's already in deep trouble. The deflation landing immediately after works well.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Okay, I made all the contacts, I pushed that little monkey out and now I'm going to be claiming him as a dependent and getting tax breaks for the next 18 years.

jokes.text: Letters? What is it, 1986? I don't do letters, lady. I'm all digital.
jokes.setup: The IRS agent says she's been trying to reach Dee for months through letters.
jokes.punchline: Dee dismisses official government correspondence as hopelessly antiquated — revealing why she's in this mess.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy — Dee's obliviousness to consequences, her misplaced confidence, all in one quick exchange. 'I'm all digital' as an excuse to the IRS is a great character-specific joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Uh, you guys all better eat a dick, 'cause Sweet Dee beat the system.

jokes.text: Your license plate says '$CAMMIN.'
jokes.setup: Dee insists she's not scamming the government.
jokes.punchline: The IRS agent dryly reveals Dee's vanity license plate literally reads '$CAMMIN' — inadvertent self-incrimination.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The economy is surgical — the IRS agent doesn't need to say anything more. It simultaneously reveals Dee's idiocy, her obliviousness, and her guilt in one devastating detail. Perfectly earned, deeply character-specific, highly quotable, and the deadpan delivery makes it land harder. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in precision and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Whatever god you're selling, I ain't buying it.

jokes.text: I would love that because I love to talk about little Barney, I do. But now's not a great time, you know what I mean? Because I left him in the car-- with the window down of course.
jokes.setup: The IRS agent wants to discuss Dee's dependent — a baby Dee doesn't actually have.
jokes.punchline: Dee stalls by claiming she left the nonexistent baby in the car — then adds 'with the window down of course' to demonstrate she's a responsible fictional mother.
jokes.explanation: The 'with the window down of course' is a perfect panic-improv detail — Dee overexplaining to seem like a good mother while clearly winging a lie. Great cringe comedy as the scheme unravels in real time.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Letters? What is it, 1986? I don't do letters, lady. I'm all digital.

jokes.text: It's hot. It's hot, isn't it? ... 3:00 sounds great. I can't wait for 3:00.
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to reschedule the IRS agent and is visibly panicking and sweating.
jokes.punchline: Dee fills the silence with increasingly desperate small talk about the weather, then overcorrects into bizarre enthusiasm about an appointment time.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe padding — the weather small talk and then 'I can't wait for 3:00' captures Dee's desperate, unnatural attempts to seem normal. Functional cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: IRS Agent
dialogue.line: Your license plate says '$CAMMIN.'

jokes.text: Because you're sleazy and we don't trust you.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are delivering a formal declaration that they want to change the bar's decision-making process.
jokes.punchline: In the middle of what's framed as a mature, serious proposal, Mac bluntly states the actual reason: Frank is a piece of shit and they don't trust him.
jokes.explanation: Good economy — the bluntness undercuts the formal framing. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: IRS Agent
dialogue.line: Uh, no.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What do you mean no?

dialogue.speaker: IRS Agent
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: Reason will prevail! / Oh, yeah, we decided also that we would say 'Reason will prevail,' every time someone says... Reason will prevail! / You don't have to say it right now... Reason will prevail!
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie announce their new democratic process and explain the motto 'Reason will prevail.'
jokes.punchline: Every time anyone explains or references the motto, the others compulsively shout it — including when someone is trying to explain that they don't need to say it.
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly self-undermining — the characters create a rational system and immediately demonstrate they're incapable of following even its most basic rule. The recursiveness (explaining why you don't need to say it triggers the saying of it) is genuinely clever and escalates perfectly. One of the episode's best structural jokes. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: But now's not a great time, you know what I mean? Because I left him in the car-- with the window down of course.

jokes.text: The first meeting of Paddy's congress shall commence henceforth.
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to have a mature democratic meeting.
jokes.punchline: Dennis adopts absurdly formal parliamentary language for a meeting in a dive bar about urinal rocks.
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific pomposity from Dennis, but it's a fairly standard 'formal language for trivial situation' joke. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Because you're sleazy and we don't trust you.

jokes.text: Like one that comes to mind is the dead dog. / What dead dog? / The dead dog in the alley. / It's been there for about a week.
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to have a serious meeting about financial corruption.
jokes.punchline: Frank derails the entire meeting with a week-old dead dog in the alley — something everyone apparently knows about but hasn't dealt with.
jokes.explanation: The casual reveal of a decomposing dog as a pressing agenda item is a great Sunny joke — the gang's complete dysfunction extends to literal animal carcasses near their business. The deadpan delivery of 'it's been there for about a week' is especially good.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Emotion will be suppressed and reason will prevail. Reason will prevail!

jokes.text: Okay... Uh, okay, sometimes dogs die. / Right. / Um, dogs, uh... die from cars sometimes. / Sometimes not. / There's also... Disease. / There's also disease in America and abroad.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are given the floor to make a rational, unemotional case for a proper dog burial.
jokes.punchline: Their attempt at composed rhetoric completely collapses into vague, incoherent platitudes about dogs dying.
jokes.explanation: One of the best sustained cringe bits in the episode. The comedy is entirely about watching the wheels fall off — the gang's complete inability to form a coherent thought without emotion is illustrated painfully and hilariously. 'Disease in America and abroad' is a gem. The long pauses inferred from the timestamps make this even better.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You don't have to say it right now, because I'm just explaining to Frank that reason will prevail...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Reason will prevail!

jokes.text: Many dogs... Goddamn it! I don't know how to express myself unless through anger and personal attack! I'm getting very upset, because I'm not saying it right!
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to rationally argue for a dog burial and completely fails to articulate anything coherent.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's breakdown is a meta-commentary on his own emotional incapacity — delivered with full self-aware fury.
jokes.explanation: "I don't know how to express myself unless through anger and personal attack" is an outstanding character moment — Charlie accidentally delivers the most self-aware line in the show while completely losing it. The meta-irony of screaming about how he can't express himself without screaming is excellent. High character integration, well-earned, and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Like one that comes to mind is the dead dog.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What dead dog?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The dead dog in the alley.

jokes.text: I want a dog funeral!
jokes.setup: Charlie has just delivered a long crumbling speech about the importance of dog funerals and rational discourse.
jokes.punchline: The grand conclusion of his 'rational argument' is a simple screamed demand — the most direct possible statement he could have opened with.
jokes.explanation: The punchline is the collapse back to basics after the elaborate failed articulation. The payoff on the cringe buildup earns it a solid score. 'I WANT A DOG FUNERAL' as a climax to a rational argument is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Okay... Uh, okay, sometimes dogs die.

jokes.text: But that dog is turning into hot soup out there in the sun.
jokes.setup: The gang is debating the elaborate compromise for the dead dog burial — candle, boom box, a few words.
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts through the sentimentality with a viscerally practical and disgusting reason to just move on.
jokes.explanation: 'Hot soup' is a brilliantly disgusting image delivered with perfect economy. Dennis's clinical, detached way of describing a rotting dog carcass is exactly the kind of dark precision the show does best. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't know how to express myself unless through anger and personal attack!

jokes.text: Dennis's compromise: a candle and a boom box at the dumpster — 'We'll light it. We'll have a boom box there and you guys can say a few words.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie want a 'proper dog burial'; Frank wants to throw it in the dumpster.
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers a compromise so minimally dignified it's almost worse than nothing: a single candle and a boom box at a dumpster.
jokes.explanation: Dennis presenting a performatively reasonable compromise that is objectively terrible is great character work. 'But that dog is turning into hot soup out there in the sun' is a great button — practical, revolting, and perfectly Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I want a dog funeral!

jokes.text: Next issue. Let's talk about the money. / Money, okay... Oh, yes, we're going to talk about the money, but we have a list of things on the docket here... And the next thing on the list is limes and how we slice them. Thick or thin?
jokes.setup: The whole point of the meeting was to address Frank's financial misconduct. They finally get to it — but Frank is running the agenda.
jokes.punchline: Frank deflects the money conversation by pivoting to lime slicing thickness as the next 'pressing' agenda item.
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — Frank controlling the agenda to avoid accountability while maintaining the veneer of democratic process. The absurdity of 'thick or thin limes' as a formal agenda item works well.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: But that dog is turning into hot soup out there in the sun.

jokes.text: What the hell?! Thin limes?! People will choke! People will die!
jokes.setup: Dennis calmly suggests cutting limes thinner.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately loses his mind, treating the lime thickness debate as a matter of life and death.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's reflexive emotional explosion over something trivial is well-timed and character-consistent. The 'people will die' escalation is a good beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Thick or thin?

jokes.text: One of the cornerstones of Paddy's Pub is thick limes. / Yeah, don't tell me... I'm going to put my thumb through your eye, you little bitch!
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to rationally defend thick limes within the new 'emotion-free' democratic framework.
jokes.punchline: Frank responds to Mac's reasonable point with an immediate graphic threat of eye violence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation — the gap between 'cornerstone of Paddy's Pub' (earnest) and 'thumb through your eye' (immediate threat) is the joke. Frank's total abandonment of the rational framework they just established, over lime thickness, is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What the hell?! Thin limes?! People will choke! People will die!

jokes.text: That's two votes against two votes. A perfect example of when democracy has failed.
jokes.setup: The gang votes on lime thickness and it ends in a tie.
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately declares democracy itself a failure because of a 2-2 tie on lime slicing.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and efficient — the entire concept of their democratic experiment is punctured in one deadpan line. Dennis's immediate willingness to abandon democracy over a 2-2 tie on limes is a great satirical beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm going to put my thumb through your eye, you little bitch!

jokes.text: Where do you land on thick limes or thin limes? And try and keep your emotions out of it even though people could choke and die.
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining the lime vote situation to Dee.
jokes.punchline: Dennis deadpans Charlie's 'people could die' argument as a legitimate concern while asking Dee to stay emotional.
jokes.explanation: Decent callback that extends the lime absurdity into a new context. Dennis treating the death-by-lime concern as legitimate is a good beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's two votes against two votes. A perfect example of when democracy has failed.

jokes.text: Are you having another baby? / No! No, it's fine, okay? I have it all under control. I just, I'm getting audited.
jokes.setup: Dee is visibly panicking surrounded by baby-related paraphernalia.
jokes.punchline: Mac's concern is not about the IRS but about another pregnancy, and Dee's 'I have it all under control' is immediately contradicted by everything happening.
jokes.explanation: Functional — Mac's reaction is good and 'I have it all under control' is an ironic statement given the situation, but this is transitional comedy rather than a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you having another baby?

jokes.text: Oh, she's screwed.
jokes.setup: Dee insists she has the audit completely under control.
jokes.punchline: Mac's immediate flat assessment undercuts her confidence entirely.
jokes.explanation: Three-word reaction beat — economy is its only real virtue. Gets a chuckle as a quick undercut of Dee's delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I just got to find a baby by 3:00 in the afternoon.

jokes.text: I just got to find a baby by 3:00 in the afternoon.
jokes.setup: Dee is explaining she has the audit under control.
jokes.punchline: Her plan to 'handle it' is to locate an entire human baby within hours — stated as casually as a grocery run.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of needing to 'find a baby' as a mid-afternoon errand is a great dark absurdist beat. Well-structured escalation from the audit setup.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: How many babies you need?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah. Just the one baby.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: How long? Couple hours?

jokes.text: How many babies you need? / Just the one baby. / How long? Couple hours? / 3:00 this afternoon. / No, no. How long you need it for? You want it for life or you...? / Just a short-time baby.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie offer to 'get' Dee a baby by 3pm.
jokes.punchline: The exchange proceeds exactly like negotiating a drug deal or contraband procurement — 'short-time baby' treated as a standard product category.
jokes.explanation: One of the best exchanges in the episode. The casual criminal logic of baby procurement — 'short-time baby' vs. 'life baby' — is both deeply dark and structurally brilliant. The escalating negotiation framing makes it feel like a drug deal. High originality, great economy, and 'short-time baby' is an instant quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You want it for life or you...? Just a short-time baby.

jokes.text: It has been decided. We are now the Pickle Party. And Dee has joined us. We are going to vote for pickles in the bar instead of limes.
jokes.setup: Dee agreed to help with their lime problem in exchange for baby procurement.
jokes.punchline: The 'help' Charlie promised Dee was to unilaterally form the Pickle Party — replacing limes with pickles and using Dee's vote as a majority bloc.
jokes.explanation: The Pickle Party is a great Sunny invention — a political party formed specifically to replace limes with pickles in a dive bar. Pure absurdist character comedy that also works as a surprisingly sharp political satire beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We are now the Pickle Party.

jokes.text: If you're not as educated or as informed, what you do is you start your own party and you yell the loudest. We want attention!
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie you can't just start your own party.
jokes.punchline: Charlie accidentally delivers a perfect satirical description of populist political movements — as a sincere explanation of the Pickle Party's strategy.
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the episode and arguably the whole series. Charlie describes the Pickle Party's formation using language that is simultaneously an accurate satirical description of real-world populist politics — completely unaware of the resonance. The 'earned vs. cheap' score is high because this comes entirely from Charlie's authentic logic, not a wink at the camera. Deeply quotable and gains value with time.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Give me a beer with a pickle in it.

jokes.text: Reason will prevail. / Pickles will prevail!
jokes.setup: Mac invokes the official democratic motto 'Reason will prevail.'
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately counters with the Pickle Party's competing slogan — a perfect absurdist mirror.
jokes.explanation: The 'Pickles will prevail' callback is a tightly constructed payoff to the motto gag. The parallel structure makes it immediately funny and very quotable. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: If you're not as educated or as informed, what you do is you start your own party and you yell the loudest.

jokes.text: It should be the centerpiece of the whole room. I mean, it should dominate every conversation. / That's gonna be terrifying! / It should be terrifying. That's how you know God loves you, Charlie.
jokes.setup: The gang is debating whether to put a crucifix in the bar.
jokes.punchline: Mac argues the crucifix should be terrifying — and that the terror is proof of God's love. Charlie's horror is the straight-man reaction.
jokes.explanation: Mac's theology — that terror is evidence of divine love — is a great character comedy beat. It's specific to Mac's twisted Catholic logic and delivers both a laugh and a character insight. 'That's how you know God loves you' is quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Reason will prevail.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Pickles will prevail!

jokes.text: I don't want a giant bloody man in the bar scaring the customers, and most importantly, me!
jokes.setup: Mac wants a bloody, ravaged crucifix as the centerpiece of the bar.
jokes.punchline: Charlie lists 'customers' as a concern and then immediately demotes them in priority to his own personal fear.
jokes.explanation: The 'most importantly, me!' pivot is a classic Sunny self-centeredness joke delivered well. Charlie's genuine terror of the bloody Christ image is a good character-specific beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Big. It should be the centerpiece of the whole room. I mean, it should dominate every conversation.

jokes.text: People don't trust you, Frank. You're a piece of shit and you're ugly and you ooze sleaze and you're very, very ugly.
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to convince Frank that he needs Dennis as a front man.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's list of Frank's negatives builds to a crescendo... and then circles back to 'very, very ugly' as if ugliness is the most damning trait for the second time.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'very, very ugly' as the closing insult after listing legitimate flaws (piece of shit, ooze sleaze) is a good structural choice — undercutting the pitch with Dennis's vanity. Good character work for Dennis's shallowness.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's gonna be terrifying!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It should be terrifying. That's how you know God loves you, Charlie.

jokes.text: 'Wolf Cola'? / Wolf Cola, that's a bogus soda distributor. I made it up. It's fake!
jokes.setup: Dennis is reviewing Frank's fraudulent shell corporations in the bar's books.
jokes.punchline: Among the financial crimes is a fake soda company called 'Wolf Cola' — the specificity of the name is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Wolf Cola is a great name for a fake soda company in a Frank financial crime scheme. Gets a rewatch bonus for being a recurring element in the show's mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're a piece of shit and you're ugly and you ooze sleaze and you're very, very ugly.

jokes.text: Da-da-da! I don't care about any of these details, but I like these figures I'm seeing. All right, I'll be the puppet and do my dance, and you can keep the goddamn details to yourself.
jokes.setup: Frank is excitedly explaining his elaborate offshore financial fraud.
jokes.punchline: Dennis enthusiastically agrees to participate in financial crimes while making clear he wants full deniability through deliberate ignorance.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's 'I'll be the puppet' framing while explicitly not wanting to know the crime he's committing is good character comedy. His vanity and cowardice perfectly coexist.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Wolf Cola, that's a bogus soda distributor. I made it up. It's fake!

jokes.text: IRS agent arrives at the fake funeral. Dee is visibly sweating and panicking. The agent asks, 'Are you okay? You're sweating profusely.'
jokes.setup: Dee is about to try to fake a baby funeral in front of the IRS agent.
jokes.punchline: Even before the scheme begins, Dee's physical state betrays her — she's sweating so much the IRS agent feels the need to comment.
jokes.explanation: Good Dee cringe setup — her guilt manifests physically before the scheme even begins. Sets up the extended cringe of the funeral scene.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He's gotta be drenched in blood. I mean, covered in blood.

jokes.text: Oh, no, yes, yes, I, um, I'm just very worried. You know, the babysitters were supposed to bring the baby back by 3:00, and where are you? Where are you guys?
jokes.setup: The IRS agent notices Dee is sweating profusely.
jokes.punchline: Dee's cover story about babysitters, delivered while visibly falling apart and psychically begging Mac and Charlie to arrive, is a great cringe beat — she's clearly lying and completely transparent.
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe beat. Dee's visible deterioration while maintaining the cover story is a performance joke — the audience can see she's crumbling.

dialogue.speaker: IRS Agent
dialogue.line: You're sweating profusely.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie burst in with a crying sound effect, holding... something. 'Crying baby! Crying baby here!'
jokes.setup: Dee is stalling the IRS agent waiting for a real baby to arrive.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie arrive announcing 'Crying baby!' — but what they've brought is not a real baby (the audience can infer this from context and the subsequent crucifix reveal).
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the crucifix bait-and-switch. The 'Crying baby here!' announcement is funny in its urgent absurdity. The reveal payoff makes this better in context.

dialogue.line: Crying baby! Crying baby here!

jokes.text: 'You are so emotional right now. And so wet, too.'
jokes.setup: Dee is panicking and sweating profusely.
jokes.punchline: Charlie acknowledges her emotional state and then adds 'and so wet, too' as if the two observations are equivalent and equally worth noting.
jokes.explanation: Very economical joke — the pivot from emotional observation to physical observation ('and so wet, too') lands clean. The flatness of Charlie's delivery makes it. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do you really want a kidnapping on top of all the other shit you got going on right now?

jokes.text: I need something. I mean, I got this, uh... this giant gaping hole inside me. And I'm always trying to fill it with something. I like to call it my, uh, my God hole.
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to explain to Frank what he wants out of their arrangement — beyond money and power.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's existential void manifests as the 'God hole' — a quasi-spiritual concept that he then immediately says he fills with sexual conquest instead of religion.
jokes.explanation: 'The God hole' is a genuinely quotable coinage that works both as a dark character revelation (Dennis has a void) and as a setup for the crude punchline. The philosophical framing deflating into 'pussy' is a great structural move. High character integration — this is very specifically Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Very, very sick baby. Very sick baby!

jokes.text: But you want to fill it with pussy. / Yeah. / Yo!
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered a lengthy quasi-philosophical monologue about his God hole.
jokes.punchline: Frank cuts to the conclusion bluntly, Dennis confirms, and Mac walks in and shouts 'Yo!' — a perfect triple deflation.
jokes.explanation: The abrupt interruption by Mac's 'Yo!' after Dennis's confirmation is a well-timed scene break joke. The economy of Frank's summary and Dennis's 'yeah' is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I like to call it my, uh, my God hole.

jokes.text: So, as the only rational and emotionless person here, I'm gonna tell you guys what we need to do. See, you've all been trying to convince the IRS that Dee's baby is alive. What you really need to be doing is convincing the IRS that Dee's baby is dead.
jokes.setup: Dennis positions himself as the voice of reason in the IRS crisis.
jokes.punchline: His 'rational' solution is to fake a baby's death — presented as the logical, emotionless answer.
jokes.explanation: The 'only rational person' framing followed by 'we should fake a baby death' is a perfect Dennis moment — his sociopathic logic presented as measured and reasonable. The pause after the reveal (inferred from the timestamp gap at 16:08) lets the darkness land.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What you really need to be doing is convincing the IRS that Dee's baby is dead.

jokes.text: Dennis and Frank conspiring while Dee's crisis unfolds: 'We can't have the IRS looking around our books. / Why? What's wrong with our books?' — Dennis covers: 'The IRS poking around our bar business is no good for anyone.'
jokes.setup: Dee announces she's being audited. The gang is concerned.
jokes.punchline: Frank's alarm at the IRS is a tell that the books are cooked — Dennis smoothly covers for him, but the deflection is transparent.
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — the audience knows about the Wolf Cola scheme, so Frank's obvious panic and Dennis's smooth cover are both funny. Functional plot-comedy.

dialogue.line: This is dark. Darkest thing we've ever done.

jokes.text: [Long pause after Dennis proposes faking a baby's death] 'This is dark.' 'Darkest thing we've ever done.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just calmly proposed staging a fake infant funeral to defraud the IRS.
jokes.punchline: The gang's response is not horror or refusal — just a quiet acknowledgment that this ranks highly on their personal scale of darkness, followed by apparent acceptance.
jokes.explanation: The gang has a personal 'darkest thing' scale and they're calibrating this against it — which implies they have many dark things to compare to. The deadpan meta-acknowledgment of their own depravity, delivered briefly and then moved past, is a great Sunny moment. The economy (two lines, complete darkness, full acceptance) is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Baby croaked.

jokes.text: Also, dude, I'm sorry, but is this the size you had in mind? [The crucifix is revealed to be enormous]
jokes.setup: Mac wanted a 'big' crucifix that 'dominates every conversation.'
jokes.punchline: The crucifix is so large it's absurd — far exceeding even Mac's maximalist vision, filling the frame of a funeral setup.
jokes.explanation: Good visual payoff on the crucifix debate. The reveal of the absurdly oversized cross at an IRS baby funeral is a strong visual gag with good callback value.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I can't cry on command.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Jesus Christ, Dee. I mean, how are you planning on becoming an actress at all? You can't make people laugh, 'cause you're not funny, you can't cry on command. What can you do?

jokes.text: You should just be happy I didn't spray it down yet. / No, you're not getting any more blood. That's it.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are arguing about whether the crucifix has enough fake blood on it.
jokes.punchline: The implication is they've already applied blood to it — and Mac wants more. This is happening at a fake baby funeral.
jokes.explanation: The blood negotiation at a fake baby's funeral is a great dark beat. 'You should just be happy I didn't spray it down yet' implies this was already a compromise, which makes the existing blood level funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: At times like this, I-I like to quench my thirst with a delicious Wolf Cola.

jokes.text: Jesus Christ, Dee. I mean, how are you planning on becoming an actress at all? You can't make people laugh, 'cause you're not funny, you can't cry on command. What can you do?
jokes.setup: Dee admits she can't cry on command for the fake funeral performance.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a withering assessment of Dee's total lack of acting ability — in the middle of orchestrating fraud.
jokes.explanation: The meta-criticism of Dee's acting abilities within the context of needing her to act is good situational irony. Dennis's contempt is well-calibrated to character.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's nothing like that... to wash away the sorrow.

jokes.text: All right, well, the good news is I anticipated this, so I brought... a bit of chili powder. I'm gonna blow this directly into your eyes, and trust me, you'll cry. / Okay, is that safe though? / Well, it's, you know, it's safe enough.
jokes.setup: Dennis needs Dee to cry for the fake baby funeral.
jokes.punchline: His solution is to blow chili powder into her eyes — which he calls 'safe enough' — presented as a reasonable theatrical technique.
jokes.explanation: Dennis having pre-planned chili powder eye blinding as a theatrical solution is deeply character-specific — his sociopathic pragmatism and total disregard for Dee's well-being are both perfectly expressed. 'Safe enough' is a great line. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You were my special angel. And only angels can fly.

jokes.text: Oh, shit! Oh! Shh-shh-shh. Okay, listen, listen, listen. Save it, save it! We're starting. Ready? We're starting, Dee. Break a leg.
jokes.setup: Dennis blows chili powder into Dee's eyes.
jokes.punchline: Dee's immediate pain reaction is shushed by Dennis who demands she 'save' her tears for the eulogy — treating her agony as a performance resource to be managed.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's 'Save it, save it!' while Dee's eyes are burning is Dennis at his most monstrous and funniest. 'Break a leg' as a sincere send-off is a great button. The callousness is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Are my eyes bleeding? Oh, my God, is there blood?! You son of a bitch!

jokes.text: It's really heavy. / What did Frank put in there? / The urinal rocks. / Oh. / Coming in handy, huh?
jokes.setup: Charlie and Mac are carrying the tiny baby's casket and find it unexpectedly heavy.
jokes.punchline: Frank filled the fake baby casket with the urinal rocks from the opening scene — the episode's first absurd detail paying off structurally.
jokes.explanation: A perfect structural callback — the urinal rocks from the cold open return as coffin ballast at a fake baby funeral. The connection is unexpected, the economy is excellent, and 'coming in handy, huh?' is delivered with perfect deadpan satisfaction. This is exactly what a well-crafted callback looks like — the absurd detail from the beginning retroactively becomes setup. High earned score.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Before you could walk. Before you could talk. And before you had the chance to get together the proper paperwork

jokes.text: Oh, this is a very sad day for the entire Paddy's Pub family. At times like this, I like to quench my thirst with a delicious Wolf Cola. There's nothing like that... to wash away the sorrow.
jokes.setup: Dennis is opening a fake baby funeral with somber words.
jokes.punchline: He pivots from grief to an in-character Wolf Cola advertisement — using the funeral as a product placement opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Wolf Cola being shilled at a fake baby funeral is a layered joke — it's simultaneously Dennis's narcissism, Frank's fraud, and a perfect dark absurdist payoff. The faux-solemn delivery of a soda advertisement at a staged grief ceremony is excellent. 'There's nothing like that to wash away the sorrow' is a great line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Wolf Cola, everyone. It's the right cola for closure.

jokes.text: It's such a sad day, isn't it? Oh, little Barney. You were my special angel. And only angels can fly.
jokes.setup: Dee is supposed to be delivering a heartfelt eulogy for her 'dead baby' while actually crying from chili powder in her eyes.
jokes.punchline: Dee's eulogy is awkward, stilted, and filled with generic platitudes — 'only angels can fly' delivered through involuntary chemical tears.
jokes.explanation: The generic eulogy platitudes delivered by someone crying from chili powder in a fake funeral is good sustained cringe, but the specific lines aren't particularly sharp. Functional cringe rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Prepare for your hearts to turn to stones!

jokes.text: Dee's eulogy falls apart: 'Oh, little Barney. You were my special angel. And only angels can fly.' / 'Good God.' / 'Sob. Sob, you bitch.'
jokes.setup: Dee is delivering a moving eulogy while blinded by chili powder.
jokes.punchline: The speech is terrible — 'Only angels can fly' is both maudlin and illogical — culminating in Dennis whispering 'Sob, you bitch' as a stage direction.
jokes.explanation: 'Sob, you bitch' as a whispered theatrical direction is a standout line — Dennis treating Dee's performance like a director while she's in agony is perfectly monstrous. 'Only angels can fly' as the depth of Dee's eulogistic poetry is also a solid cheap shot at her intellectual capacity. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's the dead dog from the alleyway. I was compromising.

jokes.text: Oh, it hurts! God, it hurts! The pain inside. God, it hurts so bad. / Okay. / Oh, my God, I'm sorry. / That's enough. / I'm sorry, I just... Are my eyes bleeding? Oh, my God, is there blood? / Okay. Oh! / Is there blood?! / You son of a bitch!
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to deliver a funeral speech while blinded by chili powder.
jokes.punchline: The chili powder pain completely overwhelms the performance — Dee's cries of 'it hurts' become genuinely unhinged, and her concern shifts from the fake grief to whether her eyes are bleeding.
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe/slapstick — the escalating eye pain paying off the chili powder setup works well visually. Dee's 'is there blood' panic is a good beat. The payoff is satisfying but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: all in favor of going back to the old system of organized chaos, where emotion trumps reason every single time and we just yell at each other to get the shit that we want, raise your hands.

jokes.text: Barney, you died too young. Before you could walk. Before you could talk. And before you had the chance to get together the proper paperwork, all that paperwork that you need to prove--
jokes.setup: Dennis is delivering a sincere-seeming eulogy for the fake baby.
jokes.punchline: The eulogy abruptly reveals its true purpose — the baby 'died' before he could provide documentation for the IRS audit.
jokes.explanation: One of the best crafted jokes in the episode. The eulogy structure — 'before you could walk, before you could talk' — builds a genuine rhythmic cadence and then pivots to 'before he could file paperwork.' The fraud motivation hidden in formal elegy structure is sharp writing. Highly quotable and structurally excellent.

jokes.text: Wolf Cola, everyone. It's the right cola for closure. Let's talk about closure, 'cause that...
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered the paperwork eulogy.
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots back to Wolf Cola product placement — 'the right cola for closure' — mid-IRS agent interruption.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — 'the right cola for closure' is a solid ad slogan joke and the persistence of the Wolf Cola brand integration at a fake baby funeral is funny. Gets slightly less impact as the third Wolf Cola beat.

jokes.text: Dude, something stinks. / I know, I know. / Have you noticed that all we wanted to do was talk about our money... and then we kept getting pushed into talking about other things? / And then when we leave, Frank and Dennis became all buddy-buddy.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie step away and discuss the democracy situation.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie finally notice they've been manipulated — which is funny because (a) it took them this long, and (b) 'something stinks' is a great setup for their eventual discovery of the dead dog casket contents.
jokes.explanation: 'Something stinks' takes on a double meaning — it refers to both the conspiracy and the dead dog in the casket, though Mac and Charlie don't know it yet. Good structural foreshadowing.

jokes.text: Have you noticed that all we wanted to do was talk about our money... and then we kept getting pushed into talking about other things? And then when we leave, Frank and Dennis became all buddy-buddy. / Yeah, there were a lot of backroom dealings going on in here, you know?
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie step out and have a moment of surprising self-awareness about how their democratic process was manipulated.
jokes.punchline: They correctly identify the entire conspiracy against them — the dog, the limes, the crucifix were all diversions — displayed as a rare moment of genuine insight from the dumbest characters.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-structural beat — Mac and Charlie accurately decoding the manipulation that just happened creates a moment of unexpected competence that recontextualizes the entire episode's B-plot. The irony of the dumbest characters having the clearest-eyed analysis is well-played.

jokes.text: "Dennis Reynolds, Executive Vice President of Worldwide Distribution. Wolf Cola."
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie find a business card while investigating the backroom dealings.
jokes.punchline: The business card is for a fake company (Wolf Cola) with a made-up title — physical evidence of the fraud they've been distracted from all episode.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying multi-callback — Dennis's earlier insistence on the business card and title, plus Wolf Cola, converging in one physical object. The reveal lands well and validates Mac and Charlie's conspiracy theory.

jokes.text: Now, we would like to pay our respects to the dead baby. And in the Christian tradition, we're gonna open up the casket to take one last look at his tiny corpse.
jokes.setup: The funeral is winding down and everyone is accepting the baby's death.
jokes.punchline: Mac announces an open-casket viewing — which no one agreed to and everyone knows will expose the fraud.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the finale — 'tiny corpse' as a phrase in this context is darkly funny, and Mac invoking 'Christian tradition' to blow up the scheme is a great character beat.

jokes.text: This is what you get when you mess with the Pickle Party. Pickle Party. Prepare for your hearts to turn to stones!
jokes.setup: Mac is about to open the casket and expose the scheme. Charlie frames it as Pickle Party retribution.
jokes.punchline: 'Prepare for your hearts to turn to stones' — Charlie's threat is incomprehensible but delivered with maximum dramatic gravity.
jokes.explanation: Charlie invoking the Pickle Party with apocalyptic rhetoric as a threat at a fake baby funeral is peak Sunny absurdism. 'Prepare for your hearts to turn to stones' is a brilliantly unhinged war cry for a condiment-based political party. Very quotable.

jokes.text: [Casket opens to reveal the dead dog from the alley]
jokes.setup: Mac and the Pickle Party open the baby's casket as a power move against Frank and Dennis at the fake funeral.
jokes.punchline: The casket contains the dead alley dog — which Frank used as a coffin weight substitute, and which Mac/Charlie are using as a 'compromise' proper burial.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and a structurally perfect Sunny setpiece. FOUR separate threads converge: (1) the dead alley dog Mac and Charlie wanted to properly bury, (2) the fake baby's casket, (3) the Pickle Party's revenge scheme, and (4) the IRS audit being blown up. 'I was compromising. I figured we'd give it a proper burial' makes it a callback to the dog burial debate AND delivers on the compromise promise from the democratic meeting. This is genuine craft — multiple storylines colliding at maximum dark absurdity. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor in structural execution.

jokes.text: Well, I'll tell you what. Dee's definitely going down in this audit. / I think we're all going down, Charlie.
jokes.setup: The dead dog has just been revealed at a fake baby funeral in front of an IRS agent.
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to the total collapse of every scheme simultaneously is simply 'I think we're all going down' — calm, resigned, accurate.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the chaos — the resigned acceptance of total disaster delivered deadpan is a great closing beat. 'I think we're all going down' as a coda to everything simultaneously collapsing is economical and well-timed.

jokes.text: Everybody in favor of Frank not making all of the decisions in the bar anymore, raise your hands. [All raise hands including Frank] Great, that's settled. Even he's on board.
jokes.setup: In the ruins of the scheme, Mac holds a quick vote on Frank's power.
jokes.punchline: Frank votes against his own authority without objection — either through exhaustion or tactical compliance — and Mac notes it with cheerful satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: Decent beat — Frank voting himself out of power amid the ruins is funny, and Mac's cheerful 'even he's on board' shows the gang still missing the point. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: And finally, all in favor of going back to the old system of organized chaos, where emotion trumps reason every single time and we just yell at each other to get the shit that we want, raise your hands.
jokes.setup: The gang has just watched their entire democratic experiment fail catastrophically.
jokes.punchline: Mac officially votes to return to 'organized chaos' and 'emotion over reason' as the official governance system — framing anarchy as a coherent democratic choice.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-structural closer — the entire democracy subplot ends with the gang formally voting to embrace their own chaos. 'Organized chaos' is a good phrase and the meta-commentary on the show's premise is satisfying.

jokes.text: I've got a few things I'd like to yell about now, so we can all start. / My eyes! My eyes! / You opened the casket!
jokes.setup: The gang has just voted to return to screaming at each other.
jokes.punchline: Everyone immediately begins yelling simultaneously — Dee about her chili powder eyes, Charlie about the casket — the chaos returns instantly and completely.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode button — the chaos resumes within two seconds of the vote. Multiple callbacks firing simultaneously ('my eyes' and 'you opened the casket') pay off the episode's running threads. The economy is excellent and the thematic closure is satisfying.

tmdb_overview: Dee faces an IRS audit over her claim that the baby she carried as a surrogate is her dependent, while the guys decide to run the bar in an unemotional, democratic manner rather than their typical method of shouting and personal attacks.
